This article originally appeared in the Fall 2025 issue of Runner’s World.
I RUN PAST Buckingham Palace and, after 26 miles, can finally see it: my sixth World Marathon Major finish line, the moment many runners dream about. After running through the arch, I am shepherded through the chute with hundreds of other marathoners. A volunteer hastily puts a London Marathon medal around my neck, and another adds the Six Star Medal. I hobble behind other finishers in a queue waiting to get their photo taken in front of an Abbott World Marathon Majors poster. A fleeting thought comes to mind when it’s my turn to pose for the photographer: Is this it?
The next day, I sit in Heathrow Airport, scribbling on a blank page in my training journal: I just did something amazing—two marathons in one week. But I feel a little hollow. It’s just all so…pedantic? Silly? I’m going home with this gigantic medal and another even more gigantic medal—and for what?
I was hesitant about running the London Marathon. Even though I wanted to race it someday, I was daunted by the idea of it being six days after Boston, which is held on Patriots’ Day on the third Monday in April. I’ve qualified and raced every Boston Marathon since 2013 without fail. Skipping a year just to focus on running London was nonnegotiable.
My partner Paul and I had already gone through an IVF cycle and were planning on going through another round. I was starting to become more mindful of how races interrupted my menstrual cycle and how taxing the effort was on my body months after. Pregnancy and motherhood would also eventually set some limitations on racing and travel. Runner’s World Content Hype Director Aly Ellis, who was also running Boston and London, spoke frankly: “We’re at that age where we want to start families; you have to take these opportunities now.”
Though the Abbott World Marathon Majors series was on my radar, I honestly didn’t really care about earning that colossal medal at first. The series began in 2006 with five marathons: Boston, New York City, London, Chicago, and Berlin. It wasn’t until the Tokyo Marathon was added as a major in 2013 that runners who completed all six would be awarded a special medal. I thought, maybe, I’d eventually win entry to these races (all marathons except Boston have lotteries) and afford to travel to those places, but it seemed like an extravagant goal.
By 2022, I had run all of the stateside majors. Riding off of a sub-3:00 high in Chicago, I researched the Berlin website and saw there was another way to gain entry into that marathon: qualifying. I entered the 2023 race with a time under 3:10, the cutoff time for women ages 18 to 44, and got in. Then, Asics, the Tokyo Marathon sponsor, offered me a 2024 bib. New Balance, the brand sponsoring London, followed with an invitation to participate in this year’s race. Suddenly, earning my sixth star seemed like it would happen sooner rather than later.
And then it happened, and instead of feeling accomplished, I felt empty.
Maybe I felt depressed because I wanted a do-over. I didn’t wear the second bib Abbott provided that read: “Today is the day! Cheer me on” with all six majors listed, ending with London 2025 in big, bold red letters. I left it in my hotel room, unable to stop the safety pins from popping off the back of my sports bra. Procter & Gamble (PG -2.12%), one of the world's largest consumer staple companies, has raised its dividend annually for 70 consecutive years. That makes it a Dividend King, an elite company that has raised its payout for at least 50 straight years.
Today, P&G's forward yield of 2.6% might not seem impressive compared to the 10-Year Treasury's 5% yield. But over the past 10 years, P&G delivered a total return of nearly 150% with dividends reinvested. Over the past 30 years, it generated a total return of 1,310%. Let's see why P&G consistently grew and why its resilience will matter during the next market crash.
Why is P&G a resilient stock?
Over the past seven decades, the U.S. has experienced ten official recessions. Yet P&G resisted those downturns because it sells essential household and personal care products.
P&G shrunk its portfolio from around 180 brands in 2014 to 65 today. Roughly 20 of those brands -- including Tide, Downy, Dawn, Cascade, Pampers, Luvs, Tampax, Bounty, Charmin, Head & Shoulders, Pantene, Olay, SK-II, Crest, Oral-B, Vicks, Pepto-Bismol, and Gillette -- generate more than $1 billion in annual sales.
PG Procter & Gamble
NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 10/23/26
By streamlining its business and focusing on those higher-growth brands, P&G steadily grew its organic sales and core EPS. But over its past few fiscal years (which ended in July of each calendar year), its top- and bottom-line growth cooled off.
Like many of its industry peers, P&G attributed that slowdown to inflationary headwinds for consumer spending. It's raised its prices to offset slowing volume, but it still struggled to grow in China and North America as macro headwinds intensified.
However, P&G's free cash flow (FCF) still grew 8% to $15.1 billion in fiscal 2026 and easily covered its $10.2 billion in dividend payments. It spent another $5.0 billion on share buybacks during the year, returning over 100% of its FCF to its investors.
For fiscal 2027, P&G expects its organic sales to rise 1%-3% and its core EPS to grow 0%-3%. It plans to pay out over $10 billion in dividends and spend another $5 billion on buybacks. That stabilization should be driven by additional price hikes, the premiumization of its classic brands (Pampers, Pantene, Tide, and Gain), and its growth in China and Latin America.
At $160, P&G trades at 23 times the midpoint of its core EPS forecast for fiscal 2027. Jim Cramer Says Reinvesting Dividends Is “Where Some Big Money Can Be Made.” Is He Right?
Jim Cramer called dividend reinvestment plans the place where some big money gets made, but the tax code and the risk of concentration tell a more complicated story about who should actually follow that advice.
A caller asked Jim Cramer something almost every income investor eventually faces during the October 22, 2026 episode of Mad Money: should a brokerage automatically reinvest dividends through a DRIP, or should the cash land in the account so the investor can invest it by hand? Cramer answered: “I am a huge dividend reinvestment plan person. You’ve got to reinvest them. That’s where some big money can be made.”
He has made this case before. In August, Cramer told a caller that his charitable trust must send out its dividends, and he said, “It has really hurt my long-term performance.” For investors still building wealth, the math supports him. The exceptions and the tax bill deserve equal attention.
How a DRIP Puts Every Dividend to Work
A dividend reinvestment plan takes your dividends and uses them to buy more shares of the same stock. Most mutual funds also let shareholders reinvest distributions automatically, according to IRS Publication 550. Most brokerages buy fractional shares, so the whole payout goes back into the position on the payment date.
Each new share then earns its own dividend the next quarter. Take a hypothetical $10,000 position yielding 3%, paid quarterly, with a share price that never moves. An investor who takes the cash collects $9,000 over 30 years and still owns a $10,000 position. Reinvesting every payout grows the position to about $24,514, generating roughly $735 a year in dividends, compared with the $300 the cash recipient still receives. Price gains or dividend raises widen that gap.
On the same episode, Cramer described sending small checks to the Fidelity Magellan Fund for decades: “The power of compounding. I never touched it.”
When Taking the Cash Makes More Sense
Retirees living on portfolio income are the clearest case. If dividends pay for groceries and property taxes, reinvesting them only forces share sales later to raise the same money. Collecting the payout is the plan working as designed. Cramer still wants retirees to keep a mix of assets: “People should always be investing for growth and some for dividend and then some for bonds.”
Manual redeployment also suits investors who want control. A DRIP keeps buying whatever paid the dividend, which can slowly concentrate a portfolio in its biggest payers. Cramer learned the cost of concentration at Goldman Sachs (NYSE:GS | GS Price Prediction), remembering that “those who owned nothing but oil stocks, including yours truly” took heavy losses. Collecting dividends lets you send them to an underweight holding or a new idea.
Reinvested Dividends Still Trigger a Tax Bill
In a taxable account, the IRS taxes reinvested dividends in the year they are paid. If you use dividends to buy more stock at fair market value, “you must still report the dividends as income.” If the plan offers shares at a discount, you report the fair market value of the additional stock on the dividend payment date as dividend income. The tax code says the dividend portion of a distribution “shall be included in gross income” (26 U.S.C. § 301(c)(1)). That tax has to come from cash you never actually received.

The energy sector is in the news today because the geopolitical conflict in the Middle East has pushed oil prices higher. This too shall pass, with oil prices likely to eventually fall, just like they have every other time they have spiked higher. The bigger story in energy is the shifting dynamics of demand taking shape. And that is why you should probably stick with industry-leading energy businesses like ExxonMobil (XOM +2.79%), TotalEnergies (TTE +2.00%), and Enterprise Products Partners (EPD +1.53%). Here's a look at each one.
ExxonMobil is big, strong, and reliable
Exxon is one of the world's largest energy companies, with a portfolio spread across the upstream (production), midstream (pipeline), and downstream (chemicals and refining) sectors. Its 0.16x debt-to-equity ratio is better than any of its closest peers. And it has rewarded investors with 43 consecutive annual dividend increases. Conservatively managed, Exxon is built to survive the entire energy cycle.
This is important to keep in mind today because when oil prices are high, investors often forget that they can also go down. If you want to buy and hold an energy stock, Exxon is a solid option. And you get to collect a well-above-market 2.3% dividend yield, as well. However, this is really about owning a company that has the scale to handle whatever gets thrown at it.

TotalEnergies is adjusting now for a different tomorrow
One of the things happening right now is a shift away from dirtier carbon fuels and toward cleaner power sources, such as electricity and renewable power. Exxon hasn't pivoted yet, but when the time comes, it should be able to do so relatively easily. TotalEnergies isn't waiting; it is starting to build a division around electricity and clean energy right now.
In 2025, the company's integrated power business accounted for nearly 12% of adjusted net operating income. Through the first half of 2026, that was down to around 8%, but only because the company's production and refining operations have benefited from the turmoil in the energy sector.

And all of that comes with a 4.4% dividend yield (U.S. investors have to pay French taxes on the dividend, but some of that can be claimed back come April 15).

Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt says artificial intelligence "is not a bubble," pointing to Anthropic's explosive revenue growth as evidence that customers are paying for technology they find useful.
"When I was CEO at Google, we set the revenue growth record. They smashed it more than twice the speed as we did," Schmidt told Nicolai Tangen, head of Norway's sovereign wealth fund, on the In Good Company podcast.
"That's real growth there. It's not fake. It's real money with real customers who are paying for something useful in their eyes."
Schmidt, who led Google, now part of Alphabet Inc., from 2001 to 2011, did not specify how he calculated the comparison.
He also has a substantial financial interest in Anthropic's success. Bloomberg reported that Schmidt owns about 1% of the company, a stake potentially worth $15 billion to $20 billion at valuations discussed ahead of its anticipated IPO.
Anthropic's Growth Comes With Enormous Costs
Anthropic told prospective investors that third-quarter revenue jumped 45% to $16.8 billion, up from $11.6 billion in the previous quarter and $4.7 billion in the first, Reuters reported.
The company also told investors it was profitable on an adjusted basis, although revenue growth slowed after more than doubling between the first and second quarters.
A draft IPO prospectus reviewed by Reuters revealed an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of 2026, including a $72 billion noncash accounting charge tied to convertible financing.
Anthropic spent nearly $9 billion on computing and infrastructure during those six months and has committed at least $518 billion over a decade.
Schmidt warned that Western AI companies could lose the global battle for customers even if they continue building more advanced models.
He estimates Chinese models are about six months behind their American rivals, but believes free alternatives could dominate in poorer countries.
"If you define losing as users, the vast majority of the world will use the free Chinese models rather than the more expensive Western models," he said.
That raises a question for Anthropic and its rivals: how much of the global demand for AI can they convert into paying customers?
Polymarket Traders See Limited Risk of a 2026 Bust
On Polymarket, traders assign 9% odds of an AI-industry downturn by Dec. 31, with nearly $2.5 million traded.
The contract requires three specified events within a single 90-day period, including potential triggers such as Nvidia Corp. falling 50% from its all-time high or Anthropic or OpenAI declaring bankruptcy.
Those conditions measure a severe industry downturn, not whether AI stocks are overvalued.
Concerns about AI spending have already weighed on infrastructure providers, with CoreWeave Inc. recently hitting a 52-week low amid mounting AI debt concerns.

Procter & Gamble (PG -2.12%) just had its best day in more than six years, with the stock jumping 5.6% on Thursday after the company delivered a surprisingly strong fiscal first quarter in a challenging environment.
During a time when many of its customers are struggling with inflation and a high cost of living, the household products giant reported 4% organic sales growth. That performance also represents a significant bounce from flat organic sales growth in the previous quarter, which helps explain why the stock had its best day since the market started soaring in the recovery from the pandemic crash in March 2020.
Organic volume was up 2.4%, and the company delivered strong results in beauty, fabric, and home care. Overall revenue rose 4% to $23.3 billion, which topped estimates at $22.8 billion.
Despite strong organic sales growth, core gross margin fell by 150 basis points, primarily due to higher commodity costs, reflecting higher oil prices than a year ago. Nonetheless, its productivity savings program helped improve selling, general, and administrative margins, and operating margin fell 70 basis points to 25.5%.
On the bottom line, the company reported core earnings per share of $2.00, up from $1.99 in the quarter a year ago, and ahead of the consensus at $1.89.
Why the stock soared on the news
P&G maintained its full-year core EPS guidance of $6.89-$7.11, and the company expects headwinds from higher commodity costs and oil prices to increase over the rest of the year.
Nonetheless, the company seemed to reverse earlier concerns about slumping growth, doing so at a time when many consumer brands are struggling. Four percent organic growth is outstanding for any mature consumer staples business, and that's the figure investors should focus on.
The news also came on a day when tech stocks plunged, and the sell-off may have beckoned more investors to rotate into P&G, which is seen as one of the most rock-solid, defensive stocks on the market.

Is P&G a buy?
The parent of Tide, Crest, and Pampers is a Dividend King, having increased its dividend for 70 years in a row. It now offers a dividend yield of 2.6%.

For an investor looking for defensive, dividend-paying stocks or a safe place to ride out the volatility in the AI sector, P&G is a good choice. I’ve always been more of an anaerobic athlete, meaning I love shorter, faster running and strength workouts. In fact, I love strength so much that even during my first marathon training block, I enthusiastically committed to three heavy lifts a week.
While strength training prevents injuries, makes you more durable, and can even boost your running economy, says Des Clarke, an RRCA-certified run coach based in Phoenix, I often spent evenings in the gym lifting weights instead of allowing my body to recover from 40-mile weeks.
As I started training for a half marathon for the second time, I decided to put more of an emphasis on mileage. I didn’t want to nix strength from my schedule entirely, but I had to figure out how to dial back my time with the weights and increase my running time in a safe, balanced way.
Doing so helped me run a 1:46:50 half marathon on a majorly hilly course. Here’s what I did to get there so you can strike a better balance, too.
How I Increased My Mileage Safely Without Sacrificing Strength
For anyone running half marathons and marathons (especially someone who’s newer to longer distances like I am), higher mileage weeks give you the base you need to run longer and faster.
“If you want to get better at running, it is true that to a point, you need to run more,” says Clarke. “You’re building the aerobic capacity, strength, and durability that you need to run those distances without getting injured.” That looks like building volume incrementally over time, she says.
Before I started half marathon training, I was running at least two times each week for about eight months. I was pretty consistent, but knew I could afford to add more miles. So before starting my plan, I added another day of running to my schedule, and then when I kicked off the first week, I tackled four days a week of running.
I also added some more miles to my midweek runs. Last training cycle, I usually opted for four-milers, but this time, I bumped it up to five or six miles.
Clarke typically recommends repeating the same weekly mileage for two to three weeks in a row to make sure an athlete has adapted to that particular load before increasing again. I did this during several weeks of my plan.
In that same vein, it’s useful to take a deload week every three weeks or so to better absorb training gains, Clarke says. This involves scaling back your mileage by around 10 to 20 percent before returning to your typical volume. My training plan also included these, allowing me recovery time while pushing mileage.
To balance this increase in mileage, I dropped to two lifting days per week instead of three, cutting down on volume (and consequently my overall time spent in the gym), which Clarke recommends. Last year during marathon training, I spent three days a week lifting weights for about an hour or more. This training cycle, I’ve spent 30 to 45 minutes lifting weights one to two times a week. I split up my usual hour-long routine into two separate days and alternated between them.
How Swapping Strength Training for More Miles Paid Off
1. I Actually Felt Recovered Going Into Every Run
I remember how exhausting it felt to spend more than four hours a week strength training on top of 35- to 40-mile weeks during marathon training. Cutting my time in the weight room in half each week (from three hour-long lifts to two 45-minute lifts) not only allowed me to fit in a few extra miles but take my recovery more seriously, too.

The artificial intelligence (AI) investing thesis has been tough during the past month, but a bundle of tech earnings can change sentiment. Alphabet (GOOG -1.08%) (GOOGL -1.24%), Microsoft (MSFT +0.66%), and Amazon (AMZN -0.95%) are some of the tech giants slated to report earnings by the end of the month, and these are the key details every investor should monitor.
AI capital expenditures
If hyperscalers say that they will continue to ramp up spending, it gives chipmakers, neoclouds, and other companies at the center of the AI trade full permission to rebound.
Elon Musk offered some good news when SpaceX (SPCX +1.89%) reported earnings earlier this month. He told investors that hyperscalers and AI enterprises have been relentlessly "hound[ing]" SpaceX for more compute. Even SpaceX is struggling to find compute, with Musk expecting the superintelligence computing capacity shortage to last for years.
That backdrop suggests hyperscalers will spend more than expected and project even higher AI capital expenditures into the fourth quarter and beyond.
That would be good news, but it's equally important to assess how each company will fund its capital expenditures. Microsoft already told investors it would achieve positive free cash flow in its fiscal 2027, suggesting that the AI build-out is sustainable.
Revenue growth rates
All this spending has to translate into positive returns to justify the huge cost of the AI build-out. That's why investors should closely look at year-over-year growth rates for the tech giants. It's already clear that chipmakers are still doing well. Micron (MU +2.46%) posted 379% year-over-year revenue growth in its fiscal Q4 2026 as demand for its memory chips continues to soar.
However, all those chips have to translate into meaningful revenue growth rates for hyperscalers to justify the increased capital expenditures. Alphabet's cloud revenue, specifically, will be on my radar. That part of the business has been accelerating a lot lately, including an 82% year-over-year growth rate in the second quarter. The more Google Cloud's revenue growth rate accelerates in the third quarter, the better it is for the AI trade.

Profitability also matters, but there are two reasons I am not looking at net income as much. First, it's normal for tech innovations to be unprofitable for multiple years before enjoying dramatic profit margin expansion upon profitability. Google Cloud is a great example, since it was unprofitable for more than a decade.
Second, net income has been murky for some tech giants due to their large investments in SpaceX and Anthropic. Returns from those investments influence net income, but don't indicate how well the underlying businesses are actually doing. For this earnings cycle, operating income is a more reliable metric than net income, because the former isn't affected by large investments that are performing well for now.
Forward guidance
Chipmakers have offered forward guidance that implies demand will continue. The projections from tech giants will suggest how they feel about current AI expenditures, and whether it is translating into higher growth rates.

The $500 Billion Question: Can Google Cloud’s Massive AI Backlog Outrun Its Mind-Boggling CapEx Boom on Oct. 28?
Google Cloud's backlog just crossed $500 billion while free cash flow turned negative for the first time ever, and Wednesday's earnings report will reveal whether Alphabet's historic spending spree is pulling ahead of its own ability to pay for it.
Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL | GOOGL Price Prediction, NASDAQ:GOOG) reports third-quarter results after the close on Wednesday, October 28. Google Cloud’s backlog stands at $514 billion, and 2026 CapEx guidance runs $195 billion to $205 billion. This report shows which one is growing faster.
Record Cloud Growth Meets Negative Free Cash Flow
Last quarter, revenue rose 24.2% to $119.80 billion, ahead of the $116.91 billion consensus. Google Cloud led again. Revenue there rose 82% to $24.77 billion, speeding up from 63% in Q1 and 34% a year ago, while Cloud operating margin expanded to 35.6% from 20.7%.
Costs grew just as fast. CapEx rose 100% to $44.92 billion, free cash flow came in at negative $5.86 billion — the first time ever — and management raised its 2026 CapEx range from $180 billion to $190 billion. To pay for it, Alphabet raised about $70 billion in equity and debt and suspended buybacks.
Reported EPS of $9.11 included a $99.03 billion equity securities gain, yet shares fell 6.89% on the day of the report. GOOG closed Friday at $317.28, down 5.83% over the past week.
Consensus Calls for Nearly 25% Revenue Growth
The full-year EPS figure includes the first half’s equity gains, which makes the quarterly estimate the cleaner gauge of operating profit.
Backlog Conversion and Margins Will Set the Tone
My first focus will be the backlog. It rose by more than $50 billion sequentially last quarter, and management expects to recognize just over 50% of it within 24 months. Sundar Pichai said in July, “We are still in a supply-constrained environment.”
Margins come next. Alphabet planned to lean on third-party capacity in Q3 as a bridge, which management said would create “modest margin pressure,” on top of Wiz integration costs and rising depreciation. You should compare Cloud margin against 35.6% and consolidated operating margin against 34%.
On spending, any change to the 2026 range matters, as does early color on 2027, when management expects CapEx to “increase significantly.” TPU system sales add another variable. That revenue ramps as Alphabet leaves 2026, with the “vast majority” arriving in 2027.
All that CapEx has to be powered, cooled, and connected by somebody, which is the entire point of a free report we put together on seven AI infrastructure suppliers that aren’t the chipmakers: you can grab it here.
Search still has to fund the expansion. Revenue there grew 17% to $63.3 billion, and AI Mode passed 1 billion monthly users. A court has already rejected a forced breakup of Google’s ad-tech business, so any detail on the remaining behavioral remedies could also move opinion.
A $514 Billion Backlog Has to Turn Into Cash
Alphabet beat estimates in all 8 of its last reports. Even so, the stock’s moves on report day ranged from a 9.97% gain to a 6.89% drop, and the market now cares most about how efficiently that capital gets spent. If the backlog turns into revenue fast enough to steady free cash flow while CapEx keeps rising, the spending case gets easier to defend heading into a greater 2027.

Former CEO of Alphabet Inc.'s Google, Eric Schmidt, said China trails the U.S. in the AI race by roughly six months, but it could still be the winner.
In a podcast called In Good Company, hosted by Nicolai Tangen, CEO of Norges Bank Investment Management, on Wednesday, Schmidt said, "I don't know that they will get ahead, but I will tell you that…if they're six months behind, then we're already losing because their strategy is that the products are free."
Chinese AI models are often free or less expensive, potentially attracting consumers in developing economies that cannot afford costly, closed Western systems, he said. Open-weight models could further accelerate global use.
He credited China's progress partly to access to advanced chips he said were "not supposed to have" and were "pilfered or smuggled" into the country. He also cited distillation, in which developers query Western AI systems and train their own models using the responses.
Schmidt, who personally owns a stake in Anthropic, rejected comparisons between the AI industry and a speculative bubble. He pointed to Anthropic's revenue growth and paying customers as evidence of commercial demand. Schmidt said that Google set a revenue-growth record during his tenure as CEO, but Anthropic surpassed it by growing at more than twice the pace.
"That's real growth. It's not fake. It's real money, with real customers who are paying for something useful," he said.
AI's Price Tag: A Risk for US Big Tech?
Schmidt echoed IMD Business School professor Howard Yu, who told Benzinga that OpenAI and Anthropic's four-to-six-month lead over Chinese AI rivals could prove "very perishable," as many users do not need the most advanced models.
He cited Tencent Holdings Ltd's WeChat agent, which quickly generated personalized guidance by scanning medicine packaging, to illustrate how less sophisticated AI can deliver practical value. For businesses, he added, cost matters, with executives weighing AI spending against hiring more employees.
In June, Polsia AI CEO Ben Cera warned that cheaper Chinese open-source AI models like DeepSeek's R-1 model and Alibaba Group Holdings' Qwen3 and Qwen2.5 could undermine the business models and valuations of OpenAI and Anthropic by offering near-frontier capabilities at a fraction of the cost.
He argued that enterprises may no longer justify spending millions on AI when comparable alternatives cost far less, declaring, "The bubble isn't AI. It's the price of AI." Cera added that AI model-focused companies could face the biggest losses, while hyperscalers such as Alphabet may be better positioned to weather the shift.
Building a resilient portfolio means thinking beyond a single asset or market trend. Economic cycles shift, sectors rise and fall, and no one investment performs well in every environment. That's why many investors look to diversify with platforms that provide access to real estate, fixed-income opportunities, precious metals, and even self-directed retirement accounts. By spreading exposure across multiple asset classes, it becomes easier to manage risk, capture steady returns, and create long-term wealth that isn't tied to the fortunes of just one company or industry.
